\hypertarget{part---brief-description-of-the-sample}{%
\chapter{Part \{-\}: Brief description of the sample}\label{part---brief-description-of-the-sample}}

This first part is dedicated to a description of the sample.

\hypertarget{main-characteristics-of-the-dataset}{%
\section{Main characteristics of the dataset}\label{main-characteristics-of-the-dataset}}

\hypertarget{total-sample}{%
\subsection{Total sample}\label{total-sample}}

2031 surveys have been completed overall. Responses with no contact information or from undocumented mothers were excluded, for ethical reasons for the latter.

\hypertarget{brief-description-of-the-participants-included}{%
\section{Brief description of the participants included}\label{brief-description-of-the-participants-included}}

Over the 1849 remaining participants,

\begin{itemize}
\item
  39.43 \% are Low-SES (i.e., no tertiary education) (N=729).
\item
  60 \% have never used ECS (N=1104)
\item
  Single mothers: 10 \% (N =159). Mothers were recruited between their fourth and ninth months of pregnancy.
\item
  Primparae: 40 \% (N =784)
\item
  Digital divide: More than a third (32\%) of low-SES respondents don't have access to a computer compared to 4.6\% for High-SES respondents. Similarly, one third (28.8\%) of mothers born abroad don't have access to a computer compared to 3.7\% for non-migrants.
\end{itemize}

\hypertarget{analysis-for-low-ses}{%
\subsection{Analysis for low-SES}\label{analysis-for-low-ses}}

Among low-SES parents, parents wanting to use an ECS are still over-represented in the sample: 70 \% want to use them compared to 90 \% for the high-SES parents The same holds for migrant families: 80 \% want to use ECS among them. Even more interestingly, even among inactive parents, parents wanting to use an ECS are still over-represented in the sample: 70 \% of inactive mothers want to use ECS.

\hypertarget{sensitivity-analyses-robustness-across-several-definitions-of-socio-economic-status}{%
\section{Sensitivity analyses: robustness across several definitions of Socio-Economic Status}\label{sensitivity-analyses-robustness-across-several-definitions-of-socio-economic-status}}

\hypertarget{education-level-of-the-mother}{%
\subsection{Education level of the mother}\label{education-level-of-the-mother}}

Mothers with tertiary education are more likely to want ECS from about 14 percentage points.

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/IntentionBinaryEduc-1} 

}

\caption{Intention to use ECS by binary level of education of the mother}\label{fig:IntentionBinaryEduc}
\end{figure}

Here is the table for three simple regression models:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  the first one estimates probability to intend to use ECS by mothers' level of education as a binary outcome (having a tertiary education or not).
\item
  the second one is the same model, but with strata fixed effects (MaternityWardXWave)
\item
  the third one is the same as 2., but controlling with a dummy for whether mothers are active (i.e.~employed, student, etc.) or not.
\end{enumerate}

There is still an effect of the level of education after controlling for whether the mother is currently active, but most of the effect of the level of education seem to go through the activity status of the mother.The R2 of the simple model with no control is quite low, but double by including mothers' activity status.

For a more fine-grained analysis, we can break down the level of education of mothers in the sample in smaller categories:

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/graphEducDetailedIntention-1} 

}

\caption{Intention to use ECS by binary level of education of the mother}\label{fig:graphEducDetailedIntention}
\end{figure}

The 9-11 category's unexpected boost might be explained by the fact that these mothers are nearly exclusively from Sub-Saharan Africa and thus very favorable to ECS (see below, to be explored in more details).

The coefficient table of the linear regression with the detailed level of education is currently hard to interpret:

\hypertarget{migration-background-of-the-mother}{%
\subsection{Migration background of the mother}\label{migration-background-of-the-mother}}

Mothers that are born is France are slightly more likely to want ECS compared to mothers born abroad. However, the difference is very small. Interestingly, there seems to be an interaction between the level of education and the migration background of the mother that will be explored in subsequent analyses.

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/unnamed-chunk-4-1} 

}

\caption{Intention to use ECS by binary migration background of the mother}\label{fig:unnamed-chunk-4}
\end{figure}

Here is the table for first three simple regression models:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  the first one estimates probability to intend to use ECS by mothers' migration background as a binary outcome (being born in a French territory or not).
\item
  the second one is the same model, but with strata fixed effects (MaternityWardXWave).
\item
  the third model is the same as 2., but also including mothers' activity at the time of the interview. Note that as Activity may be considered as a collider (it is influenced both by SES and ECS use), we should not control for it in our regressions. 3. is just for exploratory purposes.
\end{enumerate}

\global\setlength{\arrayrulewidth}{\Oldarrayrulewidth}

\global\setlength{\tabcolsep}{\Oldtabcolsep}

\renewcommand*{\arraystretch}{1}

We can see than the difference between mothers born in France and others is very small (less than 1 percentage point), but significant. The dummy created for whether the mother comes from Asia or MENA seems to be more meaningfull in terms of When we introduce mothers' activity at the time of the interview, the effect of migration background disappears. The R2 of these models are even smaller than the ones for the level of education.

We can break down the migration background into more meaningful categories: birth regions.

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/unnamed-chunk-5-1} 

}

\caption{Intention to use ECS by region of origin of the mother}\label{fig:unnamed-chunk-5}
\end{figure}

Mothers from two world regions seems to be less likely to want to use ECS: mothers from Asia and mothers from Middle East and North Africa regions (MENA).

The pattern seems quite similar if we look at fathers' region of birth instead:

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/unnamed-chunk-6-1} 

}

\caption{Intention to use ECS by region of origin of the father}\label{fig:unnamed-chunk-6}
\end{figure}

Therefore, we create for whether mothers were born in MENA or Asia, France, or elsewhere, and run new analyses.

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/unnamed-chunk-7-1} 

}

\caption{Intention to use ECS by binary born in MENA or Asia of the mother and Educ}\label{fig:unnamed-chunk-7}
\end{figure}

The difference seems to be meaningful: mothers born in MENA or Asia are on average less favorable to ECS than others, but, as for mothers born in France, there is also a socio-economic gradient of ECS use intention within the category of mothers born in these regions. The effect of education is stronger for mothers from MENA, Asia or France than for people born in other countries. For the latter, education barely seem to play a role.

\hypertarget{level-of-income}{%
\subsection{Level of income}\label{level-of-income}}

We nearly have a linear relationship between income during pregnancy and intention to use ECS after birth:

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/unnamed-chunk-8-1} 

}

\caption{Intention to use ECS by income of the mother}\label{fig:unnamed-chunk-8}
\end{figure}

This relationship is not exactly the same for family income as there seems to be more a U shaped story: when family income is very low, mothers are incentivized to work and thus want to use ECS. It is not the same for household around minimum wage that may be more in a position to afford a traditional family model.

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/unnamed-chunk-9-1} 

}

\caption{Intention to use ECS by family income}\label{fig:unnamed-chunk-9}
\end{figure}

\hypertarget{occupation-at-the-time-of-the-interview}{%
\subsection{Occupation at the time of the interview}\label{occupation-at-the-time-of-the-interview}}

Unemployed mothers (femme au foyer) are significantly less likely to want to use ECS.

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/unnamed-chunk-10-1} 

}

\caption{Intention to use ECS by activity of the mother}\label{fig:unnamed-chunk-10}
\end{figure}

No significant difference is observed according to fathers' occupation.

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/unnamed-chunk-11-1} 

}

\caption{Intention to use ECS by occupation of the father}\label{fig:unnamed-chunk-11}
\end{figure}

Education level seems to play a role only when the mother is active:

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/GraphActiveIntentionEduc-1} 

}

\caption{Intention to use ECS by activity of the mother and level of education}\label{fig:GraphActiveIntentionEduc}
\end{figure}

Concerning migration background, the difference between mothers from MENA Or Asia compared to other mothers seem to be more pronounced for inactive mothers:

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/GraphIntentionActivityMig-1} 

}

\caption{Intention to use ECS by activity of the mother and migration background}\label{fig:GraphIntentionActivityMig}
\end{figure}

Another way to visualize this difference is by doing an interaction plot of the intention to use ECS by activity and migration background of the mother

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/unnamed-chunk-13-1} 

}

\caption{Interaction plot between activity and migration background of the mother}\label{fig:unnamed-chunk-13}
\end{figure}

This raises the question of whether mothers' activity is predicted by level of education and migration. The results of the OLS indicates that mothers' level of education and migration background both predict whether mothers are active or not, but the interaction between the two is not significant.

\hypertarget{timing-of-ecs-wanted}{%
\section{Timing of ECS wanted}\label{timing-of-ecs-wanted}}

\begin{verbatim}
## 
##  Pearson's Chi-squared test with Yates' continuity correction
## 
## data:  data_full$Educ and data_full$ECSDateBinary
## X-squared = 16.377, df = 1, p-value = 5.191e-05
\end{verbatim}

High-SES mothers tend to put their child significantly earlier in ECS (X-squared = 16.377, df = 1, p-value = 5.191e-05). For instance, 70\% of high-SES mothers want to put their child in ECS in September 2023 or before, while it is the case for only 50\% low-SES mothers. Of course, this decision is likely to have heavy consequences for an effective access to ECS as most of the places are allocated around June for September.

\hypertarget{type-of-childcare-wanted}{%
\section{Type of childcare wanted}\label{type-of-childcare-wanted}}

Among parents wanting to use an ECS, those wanting \emph{crèches} (daycare centers) are over-represented: 80 \% want to use them (60 \% on the general population).

\begin{center}\includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/unnamed-chunk-15-1} \end{center}

\hypertarget{analysis-for-low-ses-1}{%
\subsection{Analysis for low-SES}\label{analysis-for-low-ses-1}}

Again, the pattern is quite similar if we restrict the analyses to low-SES mothers: 80 \% want to use daycare. The same holds for migrant families: 80 \% want to use them. Even more interestingly, even among inactive parents, the proportion wanting to use daycare is still quite high and the pattern is the same: 80 \%. Only the drop-in daycare (halte-garderies) has a slightly higher proportion compared to the general population, but the increase is very modest: 2 percentage points.

\begin{center}\includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/unnamed-chunk-16-1} \end{center}

This raises the question of the types of ECS than are known by mothers. Maybe crèches is the only structure they know of.

\hypertarget{part---information-dynamics}{%
\chapter{Part \{-\}: Information dynamics}\label{part---information-dynamics}}

\hypertarget{number-of-ecs-known}{%
\section{Number of ECS known}\label{number-of-ecs-known}}

First, low-SES mothers knew on average significantly less ECS types than their more affluent counterparts. When asked to tell us all the ECS type they knew, mothers knew 2.26 ECS types on average. But while high-SES mothers knew on average 2.6 ECS types, low-SES mothers knew on average 1.7 of them (t = -13.2, p-value \textless{} 2.2e-16).

This is even more true for migrants mothers that knew 1.7 ECS types on average regardless of their socio-economic background (t = -18.845, p-value \textless{} 2.2e-16) and for inactive mothers (M inactive = 1.6). This effect is still significant after controlling for activity and education level. Therefore, while migration background doesn't seem to affect ECS intention much, it may play a significant role in information dynamics.

\hypertarget{relationship-between-number-of-ecs-known-and-intention}{%
\subsection{Relationship between number of ECS known and intention}\label{relationship-between-number-of-ecs-known-and-intention}}

There is an upward slopping trend between the number of ECS known and intention: the more ECS are known by mother, the more likely they are to want to use ECS.

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/GraphIntentionNbrECSKEduc-1} 

}

\caption{Intention to use ECS by number of ECS known}\label{fig:GraphIntentionNbrECSKEduc}
\end{figure}

(see @ref(Appendix 1) for the detailed regression table)

\hypertarget{types-of-ecs-known}{%
\section{Types of ECS known}\label{types-of-ecs-known}}

Not only low-SES mothers knew less ECS types than high-SES mothers did, but low-SES mothers were significantly more likely to know Crèches and only Crèches (\% low-SES = 26.6 , \% high-SES = 9.2 ). This is also true for migrant mothers, that were even more likely to be in this situation than low-SES mothers (\% migrants = 27.5), while only 6 \% of native mothers were in this situation.

Strikingly, it was also the case for inactive mothers: 29.2 \% of them only knew the crèches, while it was the case for 10.4 \% of active mothers. This even though generally, inactive mothers are less likely to access a place in crèche because they don't work. Besides, inactive mothers are just as likely to know Halte-garderies compared to active mothers. Only 19.2 \% of them knew this type of structure, while this is one type of care created for them.

Interestingly, looking at the coefficients of the regressions, whether the mother is active is contributing to a lesser extent than Education level and Migration background:

The interaction between the level of education and migration background is significant, along with all the other variables of the regressions.

\hypertarget{relationship-between-knowing-only-cruxe8ches-and-intention}{%
\subsection{Relationship between knowing only crèches and intention}\label{relationship-between-knowing-only-cruxe8ches-and-intention}}

Knowing only crèche does not seem to contribute much to the intention to use ECS (see @ref(Appendix 2) for the detailed regression table). If anything, mothers born in France are slightly less likely to want to use ECS if they know only crèche (the interaction is significant, p = 0.004).

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/GraphIntentionKOnlyCrecgeEduc-1} 

}

\caption{Intention to use ECS by knowing only crèche and SES}\label{fig:GraphIntentionKOnlyCrecgeEduc}
\end{figure}

\hypertarget{cost-of-cruxe8che}{%
\section{Cost of crèche}\label{cost-of-cruxe8che}}

Relatively few people had an idea of what the cost of childcare is (regardless of whether this idea is accurate or not): \texttt{48.4}\% of parents couldn't tell us anything about the price of childcare (\texttt{62.5}\% of parents that have never used ECS). Low-SES mothers were significantly less likely to have an idea of the costs of a place, even if we restrict the analyses only to the ones that have never used ECS: the proportion were \texttt{78}\% for low-SES mothers, compared to \texttt{52}\% for high-SES mothers.

\hypertarget{relationship-between-having-no-idea-of-ecs-costs-and-intention-to-use-ecs}{%
\subsection{Relationship between having no idea of ECS costs and intention to use ECS}\label{relationship-between-having-no-idea-of-ecs-costs-and-intention-to-use-ecs}}

Going back to our qualitative evidence, we saw that not knowing the cost of childcare can have asymmetrical consequences depending on socioeconomic status. While high-SES families are confident they can afford the cost, no matter what it is (or nearly), low-SES families will be more reluctant to apply because they ``cannot end up with another bill they cannot pay''.

Running the regressions (see @ref(Appendix 3) for the detailed regression table), we see that there is a significant negative impact of no knowing the costs on ECS intention (p\textless{} 0.0005), even after controlling for Education level, Migration background, and Activity. As expected given the figures below, none of the interactions with migration background nor education level is significant.

\section{Subsidies}\label{subsidies}}

\hypertarget{relationship-between-knowing-that-ecs-cost-is-reduced-through-subsidies-and-intention-to-use-ecs}{%
\subsection{Relationship between knowing that ECS cost is reduced through subsidies and intention to use ECS}\label{relationship-between-knowing-that-ecs-cost-is-reduced-through-subsidies-and-intention-to-use-ecs}}

Running the regressions (see @ref(Appendix 4) for the detailed regression table), we see that there is a significant negative impact of not knowing that ECS cost is reduced through subsidies on ECS intention (p\textless{} 0.0005), even after controlling for Education level, Migration background, and Activity. While the interaction between not knowing about the subsidies and migration background is not significant, the one with education level is.

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/GraphIntentionSubsidiesEduc-1} 

}

\caption{Intention to use ECS by knowledge that ECS costs are reduced through subsidies}\label{fig:GraphIntentionSubsidiesEduc}
\end{figure}

\hypertarget{parentss-perceptions-and-their-relationship-to-ecs-use-intentions}{%
\chapter{Parents's perceptions and their relationship to ECS use intentions}\label{parentss-perceptions-and-their-relationship-to-ecs-use-intentions}}

\hypertarget{accessibility}{%
\section{Accessibility}\label{accessibility}}

On the one hand, on average, as predicted by the qualitative fieldwork, low-SES women significantly tend to think that accessing a place in ECS is easier than high-SES women do, but perceived accessibility does not seem to play much in ECS use intentions (see Appendix 5 for regression analyses):

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/accessibilitySES-1} 

}

\caption{Perceived accessibility by education level}\label{fig:accessibilitySES}
\end{figure}

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/accessibilityIntention-1} 

}

\caption{Intention to use ECS by perceived accessibility}\label{fig:accessibilityIntention}
\end{figure}

On the other hand, low-SES are significantly more likely to say that ECS hours wouldn't fit their working hours, and inadequate working hours are associated with less probability to want to use ECS (see Appendix 6 for regression analyses).

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/accessibilityhours-1} 

}

\caption{Fit with working hours by SES}\label{fig:accessibilityhours}
\end{figure}

(The plot is similar with migration background)

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/accessibilityhoursIntention-1} 

}

\caption{Intention to use ECS by fit with working hours and SES}\label{fig:accessibilityhoursIntention}
\end{figure}

\hypertarget{norms}{%
\section{Norms}\label{norms}}

There is a significant difference in the perceived number of family and friends that also uses childcare by socio-economic status:

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/normsSES-1} 

}

\caption{Perceived amount of relatives that uses ECS by SES}\label{fig:normsSES}
\end{figure}

And there is nearly a linear relationship between perceived number of family and friends that also uses ECS and ECS intention, with little difference by socio-economic status:

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/normsEduc-1} 

}

\caption{Intention by perceived amount of family and friends that uses ECS}\label{fig:normsEduc}
\end{figure}

We observe a similar trend if we take an alternative measurement of ECS perceived norms: the amount of family and friends that think that using ECS is bad for children. First, there is a significant difference by SES in the perceived amount of family and friends that think that using ECS is bad for children. And second, there is a significant linear relationship between the perceived amount of family and friends that think that using ECS is bad for children and intention to use ECS, with a very similar trend by SES.

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/normsEducLOESS-1} 

}

\caption{Intention by perceived amount of family members and friends that think ECS is bad for children}\label{fig:normsEducLOESS}
\end{figure}

For a related belief, that is the one in ECS returns (i.e., believing that if your child is in ECS, she will have better outcomes later), we observe again very similar outcomes (see details in Appendix 8). Low-SES parents tend to believe less in ECS returns, and parents believing less in ECS returns are less likely to plan to use ECS.

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/ReturnsEducGLM-1} 

}

\caption{Intention by belief in ECS returns}\label{fig:ReturnsEducGLM}
\end{figure}

\hypertarget{perceived-monetary-and-non-monetary-costs-of-using-childcare-versus-staying-at-home}{%
\section{Perceived monetary and non monetary costs of using childcare versus staying at home}\label{perceived-monetary-and-non-monetary-costs-of-using-childcare-versus-staying-at-home}}

While high-SES parents' intention to use ECS is very little sensitive to perceived costs of these structures, it is not the case for low-SES parents. The latter seem reluctant to apply if the perceived costs are too high.

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/cost-1} 

}

\caption{Intention by perceived cost and Educ}\label{fig:cost}
\end{figure}

Again, we observe the pattern previously mentioned for non monetary costs, and the pattern is very similar across non monetary cost types (see details in Appendix 9). High-SES mothers are more likely to perceive high costs of staying at home to take care of their child than their less affluent counterparts, be it on opportunity costs, well-being, or career. And again, mothers that perceive higher costs of staying at home to take care of their child are more likely to want to use ECS afterbirth. This tend is the most salient for opportunity costs and costs on career.

It has to be noted that While mothers born in France are significantly more prone to perceive non monetary costs of staying at home compared to mothers born abroad, the dummy being born in France or not is significant when we predict intention to use ECS based on perceived non monetary costs. However, the dummy AsiaOrMENA or else is: mothers that are born in MENA or Asia are less likely to want to use ECS while the perceived non monetary costs are kept constant, and so are low-educated mothers across all non monetary cost types.

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/Opportunitycost-1} 

}

\caption{Intention by perceived opportunity costs}\label{fig:Opportunitycost}
\end{figure}

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/WBcost-1} 

}

\caption{Intention by perceived costs on well-being}\label{fig:WBcost}
\end{figure}

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/CareerCost-1} 

}

\caption{Intention by perceived costs on career}\label{fig:CareerCost}
\end{figure}

\hypertarget{trust-in-childcare-types-and-intention-to-use-ecs}{%
\section{Trust in childcare types and intention to use ECS}\label{trust-in-childcare-types-and-intention-to-use-ecs}}

We see different patterns according to ECS types (which is good for internal validity!), and informal care types (see details in Appendix 10). Overall, trust in ECS types significantly predicts intention to use ECS, especially for trust in crèche where the slope is the steepest. While for informal care, we globally see no effect in trust in this type of care on intention to use ECS (see Appendix.

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/TrustDaycare-1} 

}

\caption{Intention by trust in daycare centers}\label{fig:TrustDaycare}
\end{figure}

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/TrustAssMat-1} 

}

\caption{Intention by trust in private childminders}\label{fig:TrustAssMat}
\end{figure}

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/TrustFam-1} 

}

\caption{Intention to use ECS by trust in relatives}\label{fig:TrustFam}
\end{figure}

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/TrustFriend-1} 

}

\caption{Intention to use ECS by trust in friends}\label{fig:TrustFriend}
\end{figure}

\hypertarget{perceived-intensity-of-ecs-needed}{%
\section{Perceived Intensity of ECS Needed}\label{perceived-intensity-of-ecs-needed}}

Low-SES mothers are likely to need fewer hours than more affluent counterparts. This is the case for low-educated mothers compared to high-educated mothers. Turning to migration background, mothers from MENA and Asia declare needing fewer hours of ECS than others (no difference between mothers born in France and mothers born in remaining world regions).

The lower the perceived intensity of ECS needed, the lower the intention to use ECS. Note that mothers that have part-time need for ECS are significantly less likely to plan to use ECS than mothers that need ECS full-time, although drop-in daycare centers (halte-garderies) exist for this very specific need. When looking at the distribution with a dummy for whether the mother knew drop-in daycare or not, we cannot detect any significant difference except the fact that mothers that would never need ECS and even less likely to want to use ECS if they knew drop-in daycare (it might reflect more informed choices).

Figures are very similar across other measures of SES (migration background), except the fact for mothers from MENA and Asia: when they have part-time ECS needs, they are significantly less likely to plan to use ECS than other mothers with the same needs.

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/ECSNeed-1} 

}

\caption{Intention to use ECS by intensity of ECS Needed and SES}\label{fig:ECSNeed}
\end{figure}

\hypertarget{ecs-ideal-entry-age-and-intention-to-use-ecs}{%
\section{ECS Ideal Entry Age and Intention to Use ECS}\label{ecs-ideal-entry-age-and-intention-to-use-ecs}}

Low-educated and mothers from MENA and Asia tend to prefer later care, even if exclude mothers that want to keep their child with them until preschool from the analysis.

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/EntryAgeSES-1} 

}

\caption{Ideal of entry age in ECS  by SES}\label{fig:EntryAgeSES}
\end{figure}

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/EntryAge2SES-1} 

}

\caption{Ideal of entry age in ECS  by SES}\label{fig:EntryAge2SES}
\end{figure}

Later entry age is associated with lower probability to want to use ECS afterbirth across SES.

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/EntryAgeIntention-1} 

}

\caption{Intention to use ECS by age of entry wanted and SES}\label{fig:EntryAgeIntention}
\end{figure}

\hypertarget{resources}{%
\chapter{Resources}\label{resources}}

\hypertarget{informal-care-available}{%
\section{Informal care available}\label{informal-care-available}}

Mothers born in France or in MENA or Asia and low-educated mother can access more informal care on average than others.

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/InformalSES-1} 

}

\caption{Access to informal care by SES}\label{fig:InformalSES}
\end{figure}

Having access to informal care is negatively correlated with the intention to use ECS afterbirth. This is slightly more true for low-educated mothers, and for mothers from MENA and Asia.

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/InformalCare-1} 

}

\caption{Intention to use ECS by amount of informal care available}\label{fig:InformalCare}
\end{figure}

\hypertarget{informational-resources}{%
\section{Informational resources}\label{informational-resources}}

Highly-educated mothers and mothers born in France have more access to informational resources compared to others.

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/InfoRescSES-1} 

}

\caption{Access to informational resources by SES}\label{fig:InfoRescSES}
\end{figure}

Access to informational resources does not seem to have much effect on ECS intention. If anything, it is negatively correlated with ECS intention (check if significant), except for mothers that are born neither in France nor in Asia/MENA.

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/InformationalResourcesIntention-1} 

}

\caption{Intention to use ECS by informational resources available and SES}\label{fig:InformationalResourcesIntention}
\end{figure}

\hypertarget{social-resources}{%
\section{Social resources}\label{social-resources}}

While mothers born in France have more access to social resources compared to others, highly-educated mothers are just as likely to access this kind of resources compared to others.

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/SocRescSES-1} 

}

\caption{Access to social resources by SES}\label{fig:SocRescSES}
\end{figure}

As for informational access to social resources does not seem to have much effect on ECS intention. If anything, it is negatively correlated with ECS intention (check if significant) for low-educated mothers and mothers born in MENA/Asia.

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/SocialResourcesIntention-1} 

}

\caption{Intention to use ECS by social resources available and SES}\label{fig:SocialResourcesIntention}
\end{figure}

\hypertarget{cognitive-variables}{%
\chapter{``Cognitive'' variables}\label{cognitive-variables}}

\hypertarget{present-bias}{%
\section{Present bias}\label{present-bias}}

Mothers born in France and highly-educated mothers have a higher tendency to choose more important reward more distant in time compared to others.

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/DiscountSES-1} 

}

\caption{ Discount rate by SES}\label{fig:DiscountSES}
\end{figure}

Present bias seems to play a role in ECS intention only for highly educated mothers and mothers born in France. Results are robust to dummification ``choose 50€ in 3 days'' and ``choose 80€ in 3 months''.

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/DiscountingIntention-1} 

}

\caption{Intention to use ECS by present bias and SES}\label{fig:DiscountingIntention-1}
\end{figure}
\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/DiscountingIntention-2} 

}

\caption{Intention to use ECS by present bias and SES}\label{fig:DiscountingIntention-2}
\end{figure}

\hypertarget{deprivation}{%
\section{Deprivation}\label{deprivation}}

Mothers born in France and highly-educated mothers have a lower probability to experience deprivation. The categories more at risk of deprivation are mothers not born in France nor MENA/Asia, and low-educated mothers.

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/DeprivHolidaysSES-1} 

}

\caption{Exposure to deprivation by SES}\label{fig:DeprivHolidaysSES}
\end{figure}

Deprivation is significantly associated with intention to use ECS only if we allow the slope ofregressions to vary according to level of education: being low-educated is associated with an increase intention to use ECS when deprived, while it is the opposite for highly-educated mothers.

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/DeprivHolidaysIntention-1} 

}

\caption{Intention to use ECS by deprivation level and SES}\label{fig:DeprivHolidaysIntention}
\end{figure}

\hypertarget{informal-reciprocity}{%
\section{Informal reciprocity}\label{informal-reciprocity}}

While mothers born in France already take more care of children of others compared to others, highly-educated mothers are just as likely to access this kind of resources compared to others.

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/RecpSES-1} 

}

\caption{Informal reciprocity by SES}\label{fig:RecpSES}
\end{figure}

We find no effect of informal reciprocity effect on ECS intention neither by education nor by migration background: Mothers that already take care of children of others are not less likely to want to use ECS compared to other mothers.

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/InformalReciprocity-1} 

}

\caption{Intention to use ECS by Informal reciprocity and SES}\label{fig:InformalReciprocity}
\end{figure}

\hypertarget{social-skills-valued}{%
\section{Social skills valued}\label{social-skills-valued}}

\hypertarget{socialization}{%
\subsection{Socialization}\label{socialization}}

Mothers born in France and highly-educated mothers have a higher probability to value socialization as an important skill to acquire before preschool.

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/ValueSocSES-1} 

}

\caption{Probability to value socialization by SES}\label{fig:ValueSocSES}
\end{figure}

Valuing socialization is slightly related to increased ECS intention only for highly-educated mothers.

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/ValueSocIntention-1} 

}

\caption{Intention to use ECS by value socialization and SES}\label{fig:ValueSocIntention}
\end{figure}

We observe the same results for Independence (see Appendix), except that valuing independence is also significantly associated to ECS intention for mothers from Asia and MENA.

\hypertarget{obedience}{%
\subsection{Obedience}\label{obedience}}

Mothers born outside of France and MENA/Asia (especially from Sub-Saharan Africa), and low-educated mothers have a higher probability to value obedience as an important skill to acquire before preschool.

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/ObeSES-1} 

}

\caption{Probability to value obedience by SES}\label{fig:ObeSES}
\end{figure}

Valuing obedience is not related to any significant increase in ECS intention.

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/ValueObeIntention-1} 

}

\caption{Intention to use ECS by value obedience and SES}\label{fig:ValueObeIntention}
\end{figure}

\hypertarget{education}{%
\subsection{Education}\label{education}}

Mothers born in France and highly-educated mothers have a lower probability to value education as an important skill to acquire before preschool.

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/EducSES-1} 

}

\caption{Probability to value education by SES}\label{fig:EducSES}
\end{figure}

Valuing education is related to decrease in ECS intention, especially for highly-educated mothers and mothers from MENA/Asia.

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/ValueEducIntention-1} 

}

\caption{Intention to use ECS by value education and SES}\label{fig:ValueEducIntention}
\end{figure}

See Appendix for additional analyses for imagination and generosity. We find no specific pattern according to SES and ECS intention.

\hypertarget{parental-investment}{%
\chapter{Parental investment}\label{parental-investment}}

\hypertarget{breastfeeding}{%
\section{Breastfeeding}\label{breastfeeding}}

Mothers born outside of France and highly-educated mothers have a higher probability to want to breastfeed, but low-educated mothers and mothers born outside of France (especially MENA and Asia) that want to breastfeed want to do it for a longer time lapse (see Appendix).

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/BFSES-1} 

}

\caption{Probability to want to breastfeed by SES}\label{fig:BFSES-1}
\end{figure}
\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/BFSES-2} 

}

\caption{Probability to want to breastfeed by SES}\label{fig:BFSES-2}
\end{figure}

Wanting to breastfeed is slightly related to an increase in ECS intention for mothers outside of France mothers and mothers from MENA/Asia.

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/BreastFeedIntention-1} 

}

\caption{Intention to use ECS by value education and SES}\label{fig:BreastFeedIntention}
\end{figure}

\hypertarget{smoking}{%
\section{Smoking}\label{smoking}}

When it comes to smoking behavior during pregnancy, mothers born in France and highly-educated mothers report more quitting behavior compared to others.

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/SmokeSES-1} 

}

\caption{Probability to stop smoking by SES}\label{fig:SmokeSES}
\end{figure}

Reduce smoking or stop smoking is slightly related to an increase in ECS intention. Although we lack power to go in detail with world region of birth, there seem to be no particular pattern according to SES.

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/SmokingIntention-1} 

}

\caption{Intention to use ECS by value education and SES}\label{fig:SmokingIntention}
\end{figure}

\hypertarget{structural-factors}{%
\section{Structural factors}\label{structural-factors}}

\hypertarget{coverage-rate}{%
\subsection{Coverage rate}\label{coverage-rate}}

We find evidence of information asymmetry related to structural factors: while the coverage rate does not change low-educated mothers' intention to use ECS, the lower the coverage rate, the less highly-educated mothers plan to use ECS.

\begin{figure}[h]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/plotIntend-1} 

}

\caption{Intention to use formal childcare correlates with higher the ECEC cover rate, but only for those with higher education}\label{fig:plotIntend}
\end{figure}

\hypertarget{access-to-a-computer}{%
\section{Access to a computer}\label{access-to-a-computer}}

Mothers born in France and highly-educated mothers can access a computer more (nearly all of them) compared to others .

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/ComputerSES-1} 

}

\caption{Access to a computer by SES}\label{fig:ComputerSES}
\end{figure}

Access to a computer is related to increased ECS intention only for mothers born in France and highly-educated mothers.

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/ComputerIntention-1} 

}

\caption{Intention to use ECS by access to a computer and SES}\label{fig:ComputerIntention}
\end{figure}

\hypertarget{months-of-pregnancy}{%
\chapter{Months of pregnancy}\label{months-of-pregnancy}}

Surprisingly, we find a pattern in ECS intention according to month of pregnancy and level of education: it starts diverging after 4 months of pregnancy. We do not find the same pattern according to migration background.

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/MonthsPregnancy-1} 

}

\caption{Intention to use ECS by pregnancy month and SES}\label{fig:MonthsPregnancy}
\end{figure}

\hypertarget{balance-checks}{%
\section{Balance checks}\label{balance-checks}}

Only differences found (0.10 level):
- Control-T1: We have slightly more mothers that want to work after birth, that value socialization, are less present orientated, and that trust daycare center (0.05) in the \emph{control} group compared to T1.
- Control-T2: We have slightly more mothers that are already active, that are born in France, are less present orientated,and that value socialization in the \emph{control} group compared to T2. Mothers in T2 value obedience a little bit more.
- T1-T2: We have slightly more mothers that values obedience in T2 compared to T1.

\subsection{Trust in private chidminders}\label{trust-in-private-chidminders}}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  First, low-SES parents are less likely to trust daycare centers. This time, both dummy being born in France or not and being born in Asia or MENA or not are significant with not controls, and then stay significant at least at the 10 percent level. ECS used is never significant. We explain low variance with these models.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Trust in friends}\label{trust-in-friends}}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  First, low-SES parents are less likely to trust friends. This time, both dummy being born in France or not and being born in Asia or MENA or not are significant. ECS used is never significant, which is reassuring for internal validity. We explain low variance with these models.
\end{enumerate}

\hypertarget{appendix---values---regression-table-of-values-ses-and-intention}{%
\section{Appendix \{-\} Values - Regression table of values, SES, and Intention}\label{appendix---values---regression-table-of-values-ses-and-intention}}

\hypertarget{idenpendance}{%
\subsection{Idenpendance}\label{idenpendance}}

Mothers born in France and highly-educated mothers have a higher probability to value independence as an important skill to acquire before preschool.

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/IndepSES-1} 

}

\caption{Probability to value obedience by SES}\label{fig:IndepSES}
\end{figure}

Valuing independance is slightly related to increased ECS intention only for highly-educated mothers.

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/ValueIndepIntention-1} 

}

\caption{Intention to use ECS by value independance and SES}\label{fig:ValueIndepIntention-1}
\end{figure}
\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/ValueIndepIntention-2} 

}

\caption{Intention to use ECS by value independance and SES}\label{fig:ValueIndepIntention-2}
\end{figure}

\hypertarget{education-1}{%
\subsection{Education}\label{education-1}}

Mothers born in France and highly-educated mothers have a lower probability to value education as an important skill to acquire before preschool.

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/EducSES2-1} 

}

\caption{Probability to value education by SES}\label{fig:EducSES2}
\end{figure}

Valuing education is related to decrease in ECS intention, especially for highly-educated mothers and mothers from MENA/Asia.

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/ValueEducIntention2-1} 

}

\caption{Intention to use ECS by value education and SES}\label{fig:ValueEducIntention2-1}
\end{figure}
\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/ValueEducIntention2-2} 

}

\caption{Intention to use ECS by value education and SES}\label{fig:ValueEducIntention2-2}
\end{figure}

\hypertarget{imagination}{%
\subsection{Imagination}\label{imagination}}

Highly-educated mothers have a lower probability to value imagination as an important skill to acquire before preschool.

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/ImagSES-1} 

}

\caption{Probability to value imagination by SES}\label{fig:ImagSES}
\end{figure}

Valuing imagination is not related to in ECS intention.

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/ValueImaIntention-1} 

}

\caption{Intention to use ECS by value imagination and SES}\label{fig:ValueImaIntention-1}
\end{figure}
\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/ValueImaIntention-2} 

}

\caption{Intention to use ECS by value imagination and SES}\label{fig:ValueImaIntention-2}
\end{figure}

\hypertarget{generosity}{%
\subsection{Generosity}\label{generosity}}

Valuing generosity is not related to SES as defined by education and migration background.

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/GeneroSES-1} 

}

\caption{Probability to value generosity by SES}\label{fig:GeneroSES}
\end{figure}

Valuing generosity is not related to in ECS intention.

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/ValueGeneroIntention-1} 

}

\caption{Intention to use ECS by value generosity and SES}\label{fig:ValueGeneroIntention-1}
\end{figure}
\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/ValueGeneroIntention-2} 

}

\caption{Intention to use ECS by value generosity and SES}\label{fig:ValueGeneroIntention-2}
\end{figure}

\hypertarget{breastfeeding-1}{%
\subsection{Breastfeeding}\label{breastfeeding-1}}

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/BF2SES-1} 

}

\caption{Intended breastfeeding lenght by SES}\label{fig:BF2SES-1}
\end{figure}
\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/BF2SES-2} 

}

\caption{Intended breastfeeding lenght by SES}\label{fig:BF2SES-2}
\end{figure}
\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics{code_Laudine_files/figure-latex/BF2SES-3} 

}

\caption{Intended breastfeeding lenght by SES}\label{fig:BF2SES-3}
\end{figure}
